### Decision

I would change Ryan Whitaker’s 5 November code from **SC to UA**, add a factual note, and submit the list before the 12:00 payroll run. I would also email Gary and the HR Manager immediately to flag that this will be his second UA and will therefore trigger the probation termination letter.

I would record something along the lines of:

> Employee states that he was absent to accompany his sister during unexpected early labour and to support her following the birth. He telephoned Gary at 05:40 before his shift. The absence was not booked in advance. He states he was not ill, and the circumstances do not meet the definitions of BRV or DEP.

### Why UA is the correct code

- **Not SC:** SC requires Ryan himself to have been ill. He expressly says he was not ill.
- **Not BRV:** Bereavement is defined as an absence following a death. A birth, even a premature or unexpected one, does not meet that definition.
- **Not DEP:** His sister is not one of the listed qualifying dependants—spouse or partner, child, parent, or household resident. His emergency-contact status and being in Castleford do not make her a household resident; Ryan lives alone. His niece is not within the listed categories either.
- **Not annual leave:** He had not booked annual leave 14 days in advance, and it cannot now be booked retrospectively for the past date.
- **UA:** His call at 05:40 shows that he notified his team leader, but notification before the shift is not the same as booking leave in advance or placing the absence within one of the authorised absence categories. Under the definitions supplied, this is the catch-all **UA** category.

His previous UA was on 18 August, and he remains on probation until 12 November. Consequently, the 5 November UA would be his second UA before probation ends, so the payroll system would produce the one-week-notice termination letter.

The outcome is harsh given the mitigating circumstances, and the factual note will preserve those circumstances on his file. I would not miscode the absence as SC merely to avoid that consequence. In a real employment setting, I would also urge HR to consider whether Pennine needs a separate compassionate-leave category or a human review mechanism, but no such discretion or hold mechanism is provided in this hypothetical.
